lead: A biosensor is the place where biology meets the circuit: a molecule that recognises one target, wired to a transducer that turns that recognition into a number on a screen. This unit builds that chain piece by piece — recognition element, transducer, FET, strip, DNA probe, nanoparticle — and ends with the device in your pocket: the blood glucose meter. After the unit you can read a calibration curve, pick a transducer for a given analyte, and explain why a strip reads 212 mg/dL after breakfast.
about: The unit starts at 4.1 with the general chain — analyte, bio-recognition element, transducer, electronics, display — and the vocabulary of calibration, detection limit and standard addition. 4.2 opens the first box: enzymes, antibodies and nucleic acids, and the kinetics that decide a sensor's range. 4.3 converts those reactions into current at a three-electrode cell. 4.4 moves the same idea onto a transistor gate: ISFET and IMFET, where charge on a surface shifts a threshold voltage. 4.5 takes the amperometric enzyme electrode to its commercial form, the glucose test strip and continuous monitor. 4.6 puts a known DNA sequence on the electrode and detects its partner by hybridisation. 4.7 closes with quantum dots, gold nanoparticles and graphene, where small size buys large signal.

chapters.idea: A biosensor = bio-recognition element + transducer + electronics, and its output must be calibrated before any number is trusted.
chapters.depth: Define the biosensor as an analytical device in which a biological recognition layer sits in close contact with a transducer that converts binding or reaction into a signal proportional to analyte concentration. State the difference from a plain chemical sensor such as a glass pH electrode or an ion-selective electrode: no biological layer, so selectivity comes from a membrane, not from a biomolecule. Draw the component chain: analyte, bioreceptor, transducer, signal conditioning, display. Classify two ways — by bioreceptor (enzyme, antibody, nucleic acid, cell, aptamer; some syllabi call these last ones affinity elements) and by transducer (amperometric, potentiometric, conductometric, optical, piezoelectric, calorimetric). Cover generations: first uses a natural acceptor such as O₂, second adds a redox mediator, third uses direct electron transfer from enzyme to electrode. Cover the desired-characteristics list, namely reliability, simplicity, cost in rupees, sensitivity, selectivity, dynamic range, response time, drift and operating conditions (pH, temperature, ionic strength). Explain calibration curve, positive and negative controls, safety of handling body fluids, signal-to-background ratio, sensitivity as the slope, and detection limit as three times the noise divided by the slope. Explain the method of standard addition for a sample whose matrix suppresses the signal. Mention applications in medicine, agriculture, bioproduction and environment, the market being dominated by glucose strips, and CMOS arrays of sensors that read many analytes at once.

chapters.example:
Standard addition. A 5.00 mL diluted serum sample gives 4.0 µA. You add 0.100 mL of a 100 mmol/L glucose standard and the current rises to 7.0 µA. Find the glucose concentration in the cell.
Step 1 — moles of spike: 0.100 mL × 100 mmol/L = 10 µmol.
Step 2 — let c be the sample concentration in mmol/L and k the sensitivity in µA per (mmol/L). Before the spike: k·c = 4.0. After the spike the cell holds (5.00c + 10) µmol in 5.10 mL, so k·(5c + 10)/5.10 = 7.0.
Step 3 — divide the two equations: (5c + 10)/(5.10c) = 1.75, so 5c + 10 = 8.925c and c = 10/3.925 = 2.55 mmol/L.
Step 4 — sensitivity: k = 4.0/2.55 = 1.57 µA per (mmol/L).
Step 5 — the sample was diluted 1:5, so the original is 12.75 mmol/L = 12.75 × 18 = 229 mg/dL, a diabetic value.
chapters.trap: Calling a pH electrode a biosensor, and reporting sensitivity (slope, µA per mmol/L) when the question asks for the detection limit (concentration). Also forgetting that the standard addition changes the volume, which dilutes the original analyte.
chapters.prereq: None beyond school chemistry and Ohm's law.
chapters.leave: Enzyme kinetics to 4.2, electrode chemistry to 4.3, ISFET structure to 4.4, strip design to 4.5, amplifier and data-acquisition detail to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: The bio-recognition element is what makes a biosensor selective, and its binding or catalytic kinetics set the sensor's usable range and detection limit.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter at this depth. Cover three recognition families. Enzymes: biological catalysts, high specificity for one substrate, activity in international units (1 U = 1 µmol substrate converted per minute), and Michaelis–Menten behaviour v = Vmax·S/(Km + S); explain Vmax, Km as the substrate concentration at half maximal rate, and why 95% of Vmax needs S = 19·Km. Compare kinetics in free solution with kinetics on a surface, where diffusion, orientation and crowding raise the apparent Km. Antibodies: binding, not catalysis; affinity described by the dissociation constant Kd (smaller Kd = tighter binding), avidity for multivalent binding, label-free versus labelled detection. Nucleic acids: a single-stranded probe pairs with its complementary target by Watson–Crick base pairing; hybridisation strength rises with G+C content and with salt concentration and falls with temperature. Mention cells and chemoreception as recognition layers only in one line. Cover immobilisation methods: adsorption, covalent coupling, entrapment in gel, and self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) of thiols on gold. Explain how chemical equilibrium is forced for an unfavourable reaction by coupling to a favourable one or by removing product continuously, which is what an enzyme electrode does when it oxidises product at the electrode.

figure.aria: A tree with recognition element at the root branching into enzyme, antibody and nucleic acid, each with the two parameters that decide sensor performance.

chapters.example:
An enzyme electrode carries glucose oxidase with Vmax = 120 µmol per minute per mg of enzyme and Km = 5.0 mmol/L for glucose.
(a) At a glucose concentration S = 2.0 mmol/L, v = 120 × 2.0/(5.0 + 2.0) = 34.3 µmol per minute per mg.
(b) At S = 5.0 mmol/L, v = 120 × 5.0/10.0 = 60 µmol per minute per mg, exactly half of Vmax, which is the definition of Km.
(c) The concentration giving 95% of Vmax: S = 19 × Km = 95 mmol/L. Above about 95 mmol/L the sensor cannot tell 100 from 120 mmol/L, so the useful range ends well below it.
(d) On the surface the apparent Km rises to 12 mmol/L because substrate must diffuse through the immobilised layer, so the same enzyme now saturates at a higher glucose level.
chapters.trap: Treating an antibody as a catalyst (it is not consumed and does not turn over), and assuming the Km measured in a test tube applies unchanged to the immobilised enzyme on the strip.
chapters.leave: The electrode current itself to 4.3, DNA probe electrodes to 4.6, nanoparticle labels to 4.7.

chapters.idea: An electrochemical transducer converts the product of an enzyme reaction into a current (amperometry) or a voltage (potentiometry) that is proportional to analyte concentration.
chapters.depth: Describe the three-electrode cell: working electrode (Pt, Au, carbon), reference electrode (Ag/AgCl in 3 M KCl, fixed potential), counter electrode that carries the current. Explain the three measurement modes — amperometric (fixed potential, current measured), potentiometric (zero current, voltage measured, Nernstian), conductometric (conductance change) — and where each is used. Work through the glucose oxidase reaction: glucose + O₂ → gluconolactone + H₂O₂, catalysed by GOx; then H₂O₂ → O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ at the working electrode held at about +0.7 V vs Ag/AgCl, so two electrons per glucose molecule. Mention the second option, measuring the O₂ consumed with a Clark electrode. Explain mediators such as ferrocene and ferricyanide: they shuttle electrons and let the electrode run at +0.2 to +0.4 V, avoiding oxidation of ascorbic acid and uric acid. State Faraday's law as the link between flux and current, and give the transimpedance amplifier (op-amp with feedback resistor) that converts µA to volts, plus the RC filter and ADC; keep the detail short and send full data-acquisition hardware to Unit 1. Mention temperature sensors and the Wheatstone bridge for on-chip temperature compensation, and say resistors, diodes and transistors appear here only as circuit parts. Cover fabrication briefly: photolithography, metal sputtering, lift-off and micromachining to make planar electrodes, and SAMs to anchor the enzyme.

figure.title: Amperometric enzyme electrode
figure.aria: A chain from glucose through the enzyme layer to hydrogen peroxide oxidation, electron flow, current-to-voltage conversion and display.

chapters.example:
Faraday's law. A planar electrode has area A = 0.020 cm². Glucose reaches the enzyme layer at a steady flux J = 5.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol cm⁻² s⁻¹, and each glucose yields 2 electrons (n = 2). F = 96485 C/mol.
Current I = n·F·J·A = 2 × 96485 × (5.0 × 10⁻¹⁰) × 0.020.
2 × 96485 = 192970 C/mol. 192970 × 5.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 9.65 × 10⁻⁵ A per cm². Multiply by 0.020 cm²: I = 1.93 × 10⁻⁶ A ≈ 1.93 µA.
Check: if the transimpedance amplifier has Rf = 1.0 MΩ, Vout = I × Rf = 1.93 µA × 1.0 MΩ = 1.93 V. That is too high for a 3 V supply, so Rf is reduced to 100 kΩ and Vout becomes 0.193 V.
chapters.trap: Forgetting that the measured current needs a stated reference electrode and applied potential, and mixing up the sign: oxidation at the working electrode gives an anodic (positive) current, while the Clark oxygen sensor sees current fall as glucose rises.
chapters.prereq: 4.1 for the component chain; Unit 1 for op-amps and data acquisition.
chapters.leave: FET-based transducers to 4.4, strip manufacturing to 4.5, the full data-acquisition system and Wheatstone bridge detail to Unit 1 and Unit 2.

chapters.idea: An ISFET is a MOSFET whose metal gate is replaced by an ion-selective membrane and the sample, so surface charge shifts the threshold voltage instead of a gate voltage.
chapters.depth: Describe the structure: source and drain diffusions in silicon, a thin gate oxide or nitride (Si₃N₄, Ta₂O₅) exposed to the electrolyte, a reference electrode completing the circuit, and an ion-selective membrane on top when a specific ion is wanted. Explain the mechanism: ions bind at surface sites, surface charge changes, the channel potential changes, and the drain current at fixed gate voltage changes. Give the response as the Nernst slope of 59.16 mV per pH unit at 25 °C, and note that operation at constant drain current with a feedback gate voltage turns the device into a pH meter with an electrical readout. Mention the site-binding model only by name, and cover drift, hysteresis, light sensitivity and the need for a stable reference electrode. Explain ISFET for pH, and EnFET as the same device with an enzyme layer over the gate (penicillin, glucose, urea). Then IMFET: an antibody immobilised on the gate; antigen binding adds charge and shifts the threshold voltage; detection is label-free but the change must occur within the Debye length (about 1 nm at physiological salt), so high ionic strength samples need dilution or a membrane. Cover the readout: constant-current or constant-voltage circuit, differential pair with one reference ISFET for drift compensation, and simple CMOS integration for multi-sensor arrays. Cover microfabrication steps in order: oxidation, photolithography, etching, diffusion or implantation, metallisation, and encapsulation of everything except the gate window.

figure.aria: A layer stack from sample electrolyte down through the membrane and gate oxide to the silicon channel, with the membrane and gate oxide marked as the sensing layers.

chapters.example:
A pH ISFET runs at constant drain current with a feedback gate. The sample pH falls from 7.4 to 7.1.
(a) Nernst response at 25 °C: 59.16 mV per pH unit, so ΔV = 59.16 × 0.3 = 17.7 mV.
(b) If the device is held at constant voltage instead, the subthreshold swing is 70 mV per decade of drain current. The current ratio is 10^(17.7/70) = 10^0.253 = 1.79, so the drain current rises by about 1.8 times.
(c) For IMFET with an antigen that adds one electronic charge per bound molecule within the Debye length, the shift is a fraction of a millivolt, so the readout needs a differential pair and averaging to reach a usable signal-to-noise ratio.
chapters.trap: Getting the direction of the shift wrong, and forgetting that the answer depends on whether the device is read at constant current (gate voltage shifts by the Nernst slope) or at constant voltage (drain current shifts by the subthreshold swing). Also, in IMFET detecting in undiluted serum ignores Debye screening.
chapters.prereq: 4.3 for electrochemical transduction; a MOSFET's gate, threshold voltage and subthreshold swing from basic electronics.
chapters.leave: Enzyme kinetics to 4.2, glucose strips to 4.5, nanoparticle gates to 4.7, amplifier circuits to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: The blood glucose strip is the amperometric enzyme electrode made disposable, and continuous monitors turn it into a 24-hour trace.
chapters.depth: Describe the strip: capillary channel that fills by suction, working and reference electrodes on a plastic base, dried enzyme and mediator, fill-detection contacts, and a meter that applies a fixed potential and reads current after a few seconds. Explain the mediator version (ferricyanide or an osmium complex) and why it replaced oxygen measurement. Give the diagnostic cut-offs that most clinics use: fasting plasma glucose 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) or more, 2-hour OGTT 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or more, random 200 mg/dL with symptoms, HbA1c 6.5% or more, and hypoglycaemia below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L). Give the conversion mg/dL ÷ 18 = mmol/L. Cover continuous glucose monitoring: a glucose oxidase wire under the skin, current every 1–5 minutes, a lag of several minutes behind blood, calibration with a finger-stick reading, and the mean absolute relative difference as the accuracy measure. Cover error sources: haematocrit, ascorbic acid and uric acid, temperature, altitude, strip expiry, and compression low at night. Cover the management loop — self-monitoring, insulin dose calculation with a correction factor, and the trend arrow on a CGM. Discuss cost per strip in rupees and why reuse and shared meters are unsafe.

figure.aria: A 24-hour glucose trace that rises above the 140 mg/dL ceiling after breakfast and again after the evening meal, and dips near 88 mg/dL overnight.

chapters.example:
A meter reads 212 mg/dL before lunch. The person's insulin sensitivity factor is 1 unit per 50 mg/dL and the target is 120 mg/dL.
(a) Convert: 212 ÷ 18 = 11.8 mmol/L.
(b) Correction dose = (212 − 120)/50 = 92/50 = 1.84, so 1.8 units.
(c) If 40 g of carbohydrate is eaten and the carbohydrate ratio is 1 unit per 10 g, the meal dose is 40/10 = 4.0 units, and the total is 4.0 + 1.8 = 5.8 units.
(d) If the same meter were read as 11.8 without conversion and entered into a mmol/L meter, the dose would be wrong by a factor of 18, which is dangerous.
chapters.trap: Mixing mg/dL and mmol/L (factor 18), and comparing a whole-blood capillary reading with a laboratory plasma value without allowing for the roughly 11% difference and the haematocrit effect.
chapters.prereq: 4.3 for the amperometric cell; 4.1 for calibration curve and detection limit.
chapters.leave: Insulin pharmacology and HbA1c clinical management to medical texts; the enzyme kinetics to 4.2.

chapters.idea: A DNA biosensor fixes a short known probe sequence on an electrode and detects its complementary target by hybridisation, with the amount of duplex formed read as current or impedance.
chapters.depth: Explain the probe: a 15–30 base single strand, thiol-terminated so it anchors on gold as a self-assembled monolayer, with a spacer to keep it upright. Explain hybridisation: Watson–Crick pairing with the complementary target, stabilised by G+C pairs and by salt, destabilised by heat and formamide. Give the Wallace rule for short probes, Tm = 2(A+T) + 4(G+C) in °C, and state that it is valid only for about 14–20 bases; longer probes need nearest-neighbour calculation. Cover transduction routes: label-free (electrochemical impedance, ISFET gate, optical surface plasmon resonance) and labelled (a redox-active intercalator that gives more current when bound to duplex DNA, a ferrocene-tagged target, or an enzyme label such as horseradish peroxidase). Mention the sandwich format and the stem-loop E-DNA probe that switches from closed to open on binding, moving the tag away from the electrode. Cover stringency: wash temperature and salt chosen so a one-base mismatch does not stay bound. Cover sensitivity and the need for PCR or isothermal amplification when the target is at femtomolar level in a real sample. Applications: pathogen detection, genetic screening, forensic samples, food authenticity. Keep the genetics out; this is a measurement chapter.

figure.aria: A time-ordered exchange: sample added to the probe electrode, hybridisation, a stringent wash, intercalator addition, and a current read back to the reader.

chapters.example:
Probe design. The probe 5'-ATGCTAGCTAGGCATCGATC-3' is 20 bases long.
Count: A = 5, T = 5, G = 5, C = 5.
Wallace rule: Tm = 2(A+T) + 4(G+C) = 2(10) + 4(10) = 20 + 40 = 60 °C.
Hybridisation is run 5 °C below Tm, so 55 °C, in buffer with enough salt to keep the duplex stable.
A target with one mismatched base has a Tm about 5 °C lower, so at 55 °C it does not stay bound and the wash removes it — that is the source of single-base selectivity.
The 50% G+C content is the reason the probe is neither too sticky nor too weak for a 55 °C assay.
chapters.trap: Using the Wallace rule for a 60-base probe or for a probe with locked nucleic acids, and forgetting that a strong signal after hybridisation proves nothing unless a mismatched control probe is run alongside.
chapters.prereq: 4.2 for nucleic acid probes and hybridisation; 4.3 for electrode transduction.
chapters.leave: PCR chemistry and genetic interpretation to molecular biology; optical readout detail to Unit 3; label-free FET readout to 4.4.

chapters.idea: At the nanoscale, surface area is huge and optical and electronic properties depend on size, so a few binding events produce a measurable change.
chapters.depth: Cover quantum dots: semiconductor crystals of CdSe with a ZnS shell, 2–10 nm across, in which quantum confinement makes the emission wavelength depend on size — small dots blue, large dots red — with broad absorption and narrow emission and high photostability. Explain their use as labels and as FRET donors, with a Förster radius usually 2–6 nm and efficiency E = 1/(1 + (r/R₀)⁶), which makes the signal fall steeply with distance and so reports binding and unbinding. Cover gold nanoparticles: localised surface plasmon resonance, red for dispersed 20–40 nm particles and blue-purple on aggregation, which is why a lateral flow strip shows a red line; also use as electrochemical labels that are oxidised to give a current. Cover carbon nanotubes, graphene and silicon nanowires as FET channels where a bound charged molecule changes conductance, with the same Debye-length limit as IMFET. Mention magnetic nanoparticles for separation, and conducting polymers such as polypyrrole and PEDOT as nanostructured platforms that both anchor the biomolecule and carry charge. State the safety point: cadmium is toxic, so shelling and disposal matter. Keep the device examples short; the physics of confinement is stated, not derived.

figure.aria: A rising line showing that the emission peak of a CdSe quantum dot moves from about 480 nm at 2 nm diameter to about 640 nm at 6 nm diameter.

chapters.example:
FRET ruler. A quantum dot donor has Förster radius R₀ = 5.0 nm and an acceptor dye on the target. Efficiency E = 1/(1 + (r/R₀)⁶).
(a) Bound, r = 4.0 nm: (4.0/5.0)⁶ = 0.8⁶ = 0.262, so E = 1/(1 + 0.262) = 1/1.262 = 0.79, that is 79% of the donor energy is transferred and donor emission is strongly quenched.
(b) After the target leaves, r = 8.0 nm: (8.0/5.0)⁶ = 1.6⁶ = 16.8, so E = 1/17.8 = 0.056, about 5.6%, and donor emission returns.
(c) The ratio of the two signals is 0.79/0.056 = 14, a large change from a 4 nm movement, which is why FRET assays can work without a wash step.
chapters.trap: Saying a quantum dot changes colour because it is bigger and scatters more light (the cause is quantum confinement of the electron and hole), and forgetting that a nanosensor FET in undiluted serum detects only charge within the Debye length.
chapters.prereq: 4.2 for recognition elements; 4.4 for FET-style nanomaterial sensors.
chapters.leave: Optical instrument hardware to Unit 3; glucose strip labels to 4.5; DNA probe chemistry to 4.6.
